keyQuotes: Multi-agent systems lose cross-agent decisions because flat transcripts and vector search both have a structural blind spot — not just a noise problem.
The context graph wins on accuracy and uses about 18x fewer tokens per query than the raw dump. That is not a tradeoff—it is a win on both axes.
If you are shipping anything like this, handling fact supersession is not optional. It is the exact line between building a reliable memory layer and building a major liability.

mainPoints.explanation: No single chunk or embedding contains both pieces of information, so similarity search cannot produce the correct answer regardless of model quality. This is the core problem the context graph solves.
mainPoints.point: Flat memory stores (raw transcripts and vector RAG) have a structural blind spot for join queries that require combining two separately stated facts.

mainPoints.explanation: By filtering out distractors and writing only structured triples into a NetworkX multigraph, the system can walk from entity to entity along relationships like DEPENDS_ON or ASSIGNED_TO, retrieving combined information that flat stores miss.
mainPoints.point: The context graph stores facts as entities and typed relationships, enabling graph traversal to answer multi-hop questions.

mainPoints.explanation: Using rule-based extraction, TF-IDF vectorizer, and substring matching for grading, the test is reproducible byte-for-byte. The graph's token efficiency (26.9 vs 490.9 tokens/query) is an additional practical advantage.
mainPoints.point: The benchmark is fully deterministic (no LLM calls, no random state) to isolate architectural differences, and the results show clear superiority of the graph: 88.9% vs 61.1% vs 50.0% accuracy.

mainPoints.explanation: Graph nodes must be linked to query language via aliases, and fact supersession must be explicitly handled (old edges removed when a predicate is restated) to avoid returning outdated information with full confidence.
mainPoints.point: Two production-critical bugs—entity vocabulary mismatch and stale fact retrieval—were discovered and fixed, highlighting real engineering challenges.

oneSentenceSummary: This article presents a context graph layer for multi-agent memory that outperforms raw history dumps and vector-only RAG on join queries by storing facts as entities and relationships, achieving 88.9% accuracy at 26.9 tokens per query.
originalTitle: Vector RAG Isn’t Enough — I Built a Context Graph Layer for Multi-Agent Memory
summary: The author describes building a multi-agent system where agents frequently fail to recall decisions made by other agents, even when full transcripts are available. After identifying the issue as a structural retrieval problem rather than a token compression or staleness issue, they propose a context graph architecture that stores facts as (subject, predicate, object) triples in a NetworkX graph, enabling multi-hop traversal for join queries. A deterministic benchmark with 18 graded queries across five scenarios compares three architectures: raw history dump (61.1% accuracy, 490.9 tokens/query), vector-only RAG using TF-IDF (50.0%, 75.9 tokens/query), and the context graph (88.9%, 26.9 tokens/query). The graph wins both accuracy and efficiency, with the largest gap on join queries (80% vs 20%). The article also discusses two identified bugs—entity vocabulary mismatch and stale fact retrieval—and their fixes, which are critical for production use.
title: Vector RAG Isn’t Enough — I Built a Context Graph Layer for Multi-Agent Memory
